title: Meet Dukaan: your first program
intro: In this course you will build one real thing: Dukaan, a shop management system. Today it is a few lines that list stock on a screen. Step by step it will grow — a database, an API, a website, a live deployment, AI features. At the end you will demo a complete system in interviews and prove you can build software from scratch. It all starts here, with lesson 1: a program is instructions plus data.
objectives: Explain what a program is in one sentence: instructions plus data.
Run a Python program and describe what each line does.
Change one value, predict the new output, and check your prediction.

concepts.title: You are building Dukaan
concepts.text: Here is the whole journey, so you always know where you are. Days 1-7: Dukaan is a command-line stock list. Days 8-14: it gets version control and tests. Days 15-21: it gets AI features, like a chatbot that answers stock questions. Days 22-30: it becomes a real API on the internet. Days 31-90: a database, a website, logins, deployment on cloud servers. Each step happens because the shop outgrows the last version — that is how you will learn architecture: by feeling why each piece is needed.

concepts.title: A program is instructions plus data
concepts.text: Data is the facts: the shop name, the item names, the prices. Instructions are what to do with the facts: remember this value, show that line on the screen. Code is just these two things written down. When you run the program, Python reads your instructions from top to bottom and carries them out. Everything you will ever build — websites, APIs, AI systems — is instructions plus data, stacked higher.

concepts.title: Your three tools
concepts.text: You need three tools, and they do three different jobs. The editor (VS Code) is where you write the instructions. Python is the runner — it reads your file and carries out the instructions. The terminal is the messenger — you type 'python dukaan.py' there, which means 'hey computer, run this file with Python.' Never type terminal commands inside your Python file, and never paste Python code into the terminal as a command. Three tools, three jobs.

concepts.title: Predict before you run
concepts.text: Here is the habit that separates engineers from typists: before you run a changed program, say out loud what you expect to see. Then run it. If you were right, you understand it. If you were wrong, you just found something to learn — read the lines in order until you see why. Do this every time, starting today.

example.run: Run python dukaan.py from the starter directory.
example.context: Amina's shop needs a stock list on screen. Three items, three prices. Read the code, predict the exact output, then run it.
example.code:
shop_name = "Amina Store"
item1 = "Rice"
price1 = 250
item2 = "Sugar"
price2 = 180
item3 = "Tea"
price3 = 950

print(f"Welcome to {shop_name}")
print(f"1. {item1} - Rs {price1}")
print(f"2. {item2} - Rs {price2}")
print(f"3. {item3} - Rs {price3}")
example.output:
Welcome to Amina Store
1. Rice - Rs 250
2. Sugar - Rs 180
3. Tea - Rs 950
example.walkthrough: The first seven lines store data: one shop name, three item names, three prices. Text goes inside quotation marks; prices are plain numbers. The last four lines are instructions: print shows text on the screen, and the f before the quotation marks lets the stored values appear inside the text. Python runs top to bottom, so the welcome line prints first. This is Dukaan v0.1 — the seed of everything you will build.

exercises.title: Change the shop
exercises.task: Change the shop name to your own shop name and change one price. First write down exactly what the output will look like. Then run it.
exercises.hint: Only change the values on the right side of the = sign.
exercises.check: The output matches your written prediction exactly.

exercises.title: Add an item
exercises.task: Add a fourth item with its price, and one more print line so it appears in the list.
exercises.hint: Copy the pattern: one line to store the name, one line to store the price, one print line to show it.
exercises.check: Four items print, each with the correct price.

exercises.title: Break it on purpose
exercises.task: Delete one quotation mark and run the program. Read the error message carefully — which line does it blame? Then fix it.
exercises.hint: Python tells you the line number. The real mistake is often just before it.
exercises.check: You can point at the error and explain in your own words what went wrong.

mistakes: Typing 'python dukaan.py' inside the Python file — that is a terminal command, not a Python instruction.
Forgetting quotation marks around text — Python then thinks your words are instruction names.
Changing three things at once when something breaks — change one thing, predict, run, observe.
fde: In a software house, a junior's first tickets look exactly like this: small, clear, testable. 'Show the stock list on screen.' Senior engineers trust juniors who write small programs they can explain line by line. That is what you practiced today — the atom of the job. Every system you will ever build is made of atoms like this one.

title: The price list
intro: Dukaan v0.1 shows the stock list. Today it grows into v0.2: a bill calculator. A customer buys 3 bags of rice and 2 of sugar - the program multiplies, adds, and works out the change. The new idea is small, and getting it wrong breaks everything: text and numbers are different things, and the shopkeeper's typed input always arrives as text. Convert it, or the bill is nonsense.
objectives: Explain the difference between text and numbers with a shop example.
Use *, +, and - to compute a bill total and the change.
Convert typed input from text to a number with int() before doing arithmetic.

concepts.title: Text and numbers look the same but behave differently
concepts.text: The price 250 and the text "250" look identical on your screen. To Python they are different things. 250 + 180 is 430 - arithmetic. "250" + "180" is "250180" - gluing text together. Text sticks; numbers calculate. A price you want to multiply must be a number, not text. Python calls text str (short for string, like a string of characters) and whole numbers int (short for integer). When output looks wrong - a total of 250180 instead of 430 - your first suspect is always: text where a number should be.

concepts.title: Bills are arithmetic
concepts.text: A bill is three operations. Multiply: price times quantity for each item. Add: the line totals into a grand total. Subtract: money paid minus the total gives the change. Python writes them as *, +, and -. Order matters: Python multiplies before it adds, exactly like the maths you learned in school, so 250 * 3 + 180 * 2 means (250 * 3) + (180 * 2). When in doubt, add brackets - they cost nothing and prevent real money mistakes.

concepts.title: input() always gives you text
concepts.text: When a program asks the shopkeeper to type a quantity, the answer arrives as text - even if they typed digits. "3" is text, and "3" * 2 is "33", not 6. So the first thing you do with typed input is convert it: int("3") turns the text into the number 3, and then you can multiply. If the text is not a number - int("three") - Python stops and shows an error naming the line. That error is useful information, not a disaster: it tells you exactly what went wrong. On Day 7 you will learn to catch it gracefully instead of crashing.

example.run: Run python bill.py from the starter directory.
example.context: Amina's customer buys rice and sugar. The quantities were typed by the shopkeeper, so they arrive as text. Read the code, predict the exact output - especially the change - then run it.
example.code:
price_rice = 250
price_sugar = 180

typed_rice_qty = "3"
typed_sugar_qty = "2"

qty_rice = int(typed_rice_qty)
qty_sugar = int(typed_sugar_qty)

rice_total = price_rice * qty_rice
sugar_total = price_sugar * qty_sugar
total = rice_total + sugar_total

paid = 2000
change = paid - total

print(f"Rice: {qty_rice} x Rs {price_rice} = Rs {rice_total}")
print(f"Sugar: {qty_sugar} x Rs {price_sugar} = Rs {sugar_total}")
print(f"Total: Rs {total}")
print(f"Paid Rs {paid}, change Rs {change}")
example.output:
Rice: 3 x Rs 250 = Rs 750
Sugar: 2 x Rs 180 = Rs 360
Total: Rs 1110
Paid Rs 2000, change Rs 890
example.walkthrough: The first two lines store prices as numbers. The next two store the typed quantities as text - this is what input() really gives you. int() converts each one into a real number. The line totals are price times quantity; adding them gives the grand total, 1110. Change is paid minus total: 2000 - 1110 = 890. If you skip the int() conversion, "3" * 250 does not multiply - it repeats the text "3" two hundred and fifty times. That is why conversion comes before arithmetic, every time.

exercises.title: Predict the trap
exercises.task: In a scratch file, run print("2" + "2") and print(2 + 2). Before each one, write down what you expect to see.
exercises.check: You predicted "22" for the text version and 4 for the number version before running.

exercises.title: A tea bill
exercises.task: A customer buys 2 packs of Tea (Rs 950 each) and pays Rs 2000. Write the lines that compute the total and the change. Predict both numbers, then run.
exercises.hint: Copy the pattern: line total, then paid minus total.
exercises.check: Total is Rs 1900 and change is Rs 100, matching your prediction.

exercises.title: Break the conversion
exercises.task: Change typed_rice_qty to "three" and run. Read the error: which line does it blame, and what does ValueError mean in your own words? Then change it back.
exercises.hint: ValueError means "this value cannot become a number".
exercises.check: You can explain why int("three") fails without re-reading the message.

mistakes: Forgetting int() on typed input - then "3" * 250 repeats text instead of multiplying.
Using + on two pieces of text when you meant to add numbers - "250" + "180" is "250180", not 430.
Trying int() on text like "3kg" or "three" - only pure digit text converts; anything else is an error.
fde: In a software house, junior tickets are full of this. "Add a totals row to the receipt" is a feature ticket. "The discount shows 250180 instead of 430 - fix it" is a bug ticket, and it is a text-vs-number bug. Seniors trust juniors who look at wrong output and name the cause in ten seconds. Today you earned that instinct: when numbers look glued together, suspect text.

title: The smart stock check
intro: Amina has two morning jobs. One: check every item's stock and flag what is low. Two: apply the Friday rule - bills above Rs 1000 get 10% off. Writing each check by hand means one block per item, and next month there will be thirty items. Today Dukaan v0.3 learns the two halves of real work: decisions (ask a yes/no question) and loops (repeat the check for every item). One loop, one decision inside it, and the whole shop gets checked.
objectives: Write if/elif/else decisions that apply business rules like discounts and stock alerts.
Use a for loop to run the same check once per item, however many items there are.
Combine a loop with a decision so every item is checked automatically.

concepts.title: Decisions are yes/no questions
concepts.text: A shopkeeper decides all day: is the bill big enough for a discount? Is the stock too low? In code, each decision is a question with two answers - yes or no - written with if. The lines indented under if run only when the answer is yes. The lines under else run when the answer is no. Indentation is not decoration; it is how Python knows which lines belong to the decision. Rules with two questions use and (both must be yes) or or (one yes is enough): "bill above 2000 AND it is Friday" needs both; "tea is low OR sugar is low" needs one.

concepts.title: Comparisons ask, == is not =
concepts.text: total > 1000 asks "is the total above 1000?" The answer is True (yes) or False (no). Watch the boundary: with >, a total of exactly 1000 gets no discount - the question is "strictly above". With >=, exactly 1000 would qualify. Real bugs live on boundaries, so always test the exact boundary value. And == (two equals signs) compares; = (one equals sign) stores. Mixing them up is the most common beginner error in every country: "if total = 1000" is always wrong.

concepts.title: Repeating beats copying
concepts.text: Without a loop, checking three items means writing the check three times. Thirty items means thirty copies - and the day you fix a bug, you must fix it thirty times. A for loop says: "here is the job; do it once per value." You write the check once, and Python repeats it for every item. Fewer copies, fewer mistakes, and adding a fourth item changes nothing in the loop.

concepts.title: for walks through a row of values
concepts.text: A list is values in a row inside square brackets: prices = [250, 180, 950]. (You will master lists on Day 5; today just borrow the idea.) "for price in prices:" means "take each value in turn, call it price, and run the block." First round price is 250, then 180, then 950 - then the loop ends. The block is the indented lines, just like with if. Two more tools for later: range(3) counts 0, 1, 2 for a fixed number of rounds, and while repeats until its question turns false - but a while loop must change its answer inside the block, or it never stops.

example.run: Run python smartcheck.py from the starter directory.
example.context: Amina's two morning jobs in one program: a loop checks every item's stock and flags what is low, then one decision applies the Friday discount to a Rs 1200 bill. Predict every printed line before you run - especially which items get flagged.
example.output:
Morning stock check:
Rice: Rs 250 - LOW STOCK, order more!
Sugar: Rs 180 - OK
Tea: Rs 950 - LOW STOCK, order more!
Bill: Rs 1200, discount: Rs 120.0, to pay: Rs 1080.0
example.walkthrough: The loop runs three rounds with i = 0, 1, 2. Round 0: stocks[0] is 40, below 50, so Rice gets the LOW STOCK line. Round 1: stocks[1] is 90, so Sugar gets OK. Round 2: stocks[2] is 25, so Tea is flagged. Then the decision: 1200 > 1000 is True, so discount = 120.0 (division always gives a decimal number: 120.0). To pay is 1200 - 120.0 = 1080.0. Now predict: with total = 1000, the discount question is False - no discount. That boundary is where real discount bugs hide.

exercises.hint: The rule says "above 1000", not "1000 or above".
exercises.check: Rs 0 discount at 1000, Rs 100.1 at 1001 - both predicted before running.

exercises.title: Count the alerts
exercises.task: Add a counter that counts how many items are LOW STOCK, and print the count after the loop.
exercises.hint: Create low = 0 before the loop; add 1 inside the LOW STOCK branch.
exercises.check: The count is 2 for the starter stocks.

exercises.title: Add a fourth item
exercises.task: Add "Flour", 120, 60 to the three lists and change range(3) to range(4). Predict the new lines, then run.
exercises.hint: All three lists and the range must agree on 4.
exercises.check: Four status lines print; no other code changed.

mistakes: Writing = when you mean == - one stores a value, two compares.
Forgetting the colon after the if or for line - Python needs it to start a block.
Wrong indentation - a line that looks inside the block but is not indented runs every time (or never, inside a loop).
range(3) with four items - the loop only visits the first three. The range and the lists must agree.
fde: Two of the most common junior tickets arrive together: "apply this business rule" and "do it for every row". Business rules change constantly - "discount now starts at Rs 1500" - and seniors always ask "what happens at exactly the threshold?" Every-row work is always a loop; copy-pasting thirty checks is thirty chances to break. Today you practiced both halves of real tickets: the decision and the repetition.

title: The reusable counter
intro: Dukaan now computes totals, discounts, and stock checks - but the same small jobs are scattered everywhere: "price times quantity" appears in the bill, in the stock value, in the report. When Amina changes a rule, you must hunt down every copy. Today v0.4 gets organized: each repeated job becomes a function - a named, reusable piece with inputs and an answer.
objectives: Define a function with def that packages one job under one name.
Pass inputs as parameters and get answers back with return.
Explain the difference between printing a value and returning it.

concepts.title: A function is a job with a name
concepts.text: def total_value(price, qty): creates a reusable job called total_value. The indented lines are the job's instructions - they only run when you call the function by name: total_value(250, 40). You write the logic once and use it ten times. When the rule changes, you change it in one place. That is the whole point: one definition, many uses. Name it after the job it does, not after how it does it.

concepts.title: Parameters in, return out
concepts.text: price and qty are parameters - empty slots that get filled each time you call. return sends the answer back to the caller: rice_value = total_value(250, 40) stores 10000 in rice_value. Contrast this with print: print shows a value on the screen and gives back nothing. A function that prints its answer cannot be reused in a calculation - you cannot add up printed lines. Return the answer; let the caller decide whether to print it.

concepts.title: True and False are answers too
concepts.text: is_low_stock(40) answers a yes/no question, so it returns True or False. True and False are Python's words for yes and no - they are values, just like numbers. You can store them, print them, and use them directly in an if: "if is_low_stock(stock):" reads almost like English. Functions that answer questions make decisions readable, and readable code is code the team trusts.

example.run: Run python counter.py from the starter directory.
example.context: Amina wants two reusable jobs: the value of some stock (price times quantity) and a low-stock test. Read the code, predict all four printed lines, then run.
example.code:
def total_value(price, qty):
    return price * qty

def is_low_stock(stock):
    return stock < 50

rice_value = total_value(250, 40)
sugar_value = total_value(180, 90)

print(f"Rice stock value: Rs {rice_value}")
print(f"Sugar stock value: Rs {sugar_value}")
print(f"Rice low? {is_low_stock(40)}")
print(f"Sugar low? {is_low_stock(90)}")
example.output:
Rice stock value: Rs 10000
Sugar stock value: Rs 16200
Rice low? True
Sugar low? False
example.walkthrough: The two def blocks define jobs but run nothing yet - defining is not calling. total_value(250, 40) fills price with 250 and qty with 40, computes 10000, and return hands it back to be stored in rice_value. is_low_stock(40) asks "40 < 50?" - True. is_low_stock(90) asks "90 < 50?" - False. Notice the callers never see inside the functions; they only know the name, the inputs, and the answer. That separation is what lets you reuse code and change it safely.

exercises.title: A bill-line function
exercises.task: Write bill_line(price, qty) that returns price times qty. Call it for (950, 2) and (180, 5). Predict both answers, then run.
exercises.hint: One def, one return, two calls.

exercises.title: Return vs print
exercises.task: Write a version of total_value that prints the answer instead of returning it. Then try adding two calls together. What happens, and why?
exercises.hint: A function with no return gives back a special value called None.
exercises.check: You can explain why adding returned values works but adding printed output fails.

exercises.title: Reuse three times
exercises.task: Use total_value three times - rice, sugar, tea - and add the three answers into stock_worth. Predict the total, then run.
exercises.check: Rs 49950, matching your prediction. One function, three uses.

mistakes: Calling a function before defining it - Python reads top to bottom, so def must come first.
Forgetting return - the function then gives back None, and None + 5 is an error.
Printing inside the function instead of returning - then the answer cannot be reused in maths.
fde: In code review, seniors constantly say: "extract this into a function - you wrote it three times." Duplicated logic is how real bugs are born: the discount gets fixed in the bill but not in the report. Juniors who name small jobs well - total_value, is_low_stock - write code the whole team can read. Today's project is your first refactor: same behavior, better shape. That word will follow you for your whole career.

Nothing the user sees changes; everything about the code gets better.

If Amina adds a "damaged goods" discount, which function would change - and which would not?

title: The real stock book
intro: Three separate lists - names, prices, quantities - are an accident waiting to happen: delete from one list and forget the others, and rice gets sugar's price. Real programs keep each item's facts together. Today Dukaan v0.5 gets a real stock book: a list of dictionaries, where every item is one labeled bundle. Add, remove, and search - the way real data works.
objectives: Store ordered values in a list and grow it with append().
Label values with a dictionary so item["price"] replaces price1.
Build and search a list of dictionaries as a tiny in-memory database.

concepts.title: A list keeps things in order
concepts.text: A list is values in a row: names = ["Rice", "Sugar", "Tea"]. Positions start at 0: names[0] is "Rice". append() adds to the end, so the list grows without you rewriting it. len() tells you how many values there are. Lists are for "many of the same kind of thing" - many items, many prices, many customers. One row, one idea.

concepts.title: A dictionary labels each value
concepts.text: A dictionary is values with name tags: item = {"name": "Rice", "price": 250, "qty": 40}. You read a value by its label: item["price"] gives 250. Labels beat positions: item["price"] still works if you add new labels later, while "the second value" breaks the moment the order changes. Use the wrong label - item["cost"] - and Python answers with a KeyError: the label does not exist. Label spelling must match exactly, including capitals.

concepts.title: A list of dictionaries is a tiny database
concepts.text: Put the bundles in a row: stock = [{"name": "Rice", ...}, {"name": "Sugar", ...}]. Now each item's facts travel together - deleting one item deletes all its facts at once, and nothing can desynchronize. To find something, loop and check labels: "if item["name"] == "Tea":" - the same loop-plus-decision pattern from Day 3, now with labeled data. This shape - a list of labeled records - is how almost all real data looks, including the JSON you will save on Day 6.

example.run: Run python stockbook.py from the starter directory.
example.context: Amina's stock book: three items as labeled bundles in a list. Add flour, find tea, count the book. Predict the two printed lines before you run.
example.output:
Found Tea: Rs 950, qty 25
Items in the stock book: 4
example.walkthrough: stock starts as a list of three dictionaries - three bundles in a row. append() adds a fourth bundle at the end; the list is now four long, and nothing else had to change. The loop takes each bundle in turn and checks its "name" label; only Tea's bundle matches, so only one line prints. len(stock) counts the bundles: 4, because the appended flour counts. Predict first: if you searched for "Bread" instead, nothing would print - the loop would simply find no match, which is also the answer to "how do I know it is missing?"

exercises.title: Remove an item
exercises.task: Remove Sugar by building a new list with only the items you want to keep. Predict the length, then print it.
exercises.hint: Loop over stock; append each item whose name is not "Sugar" to a new list.
exercises.check: Length is 3 after removal; rice, tea, and flour remain.

exercises.title: Change a price by label
exercises.task: Raise Tea's price to 1000: loop, match the name, assign item["price"] = 1000. Print the book after.
exercises.hint: Loop, match the name, assign to the label.
exercises.check: Tea shows Rs 1000; every other item is unchanged.

exercises.title: Count the stock value
exercises.task: Loop over the book and add up price times qty for every bundle. Predict the total first.
exercises.hint: total = 0 before the loop; inside: total = total + item["price"] * item["qty"].

mistakes: Using item["Price"] instead of item["price"] - labels are case-sensitive; KeyError means the label does not exist.
Forgetting that positions start at 0 - stock[3] on a 3-item list is an error.
Keeping three parallel lists instead of bundles - one deletion desynchronizes everything.
fde: Almost every junior ticket touches labeled data: "the API returns a list of orders - show each customer's total." That API data arrives as JSON, which looks exactly like Python dictionaries in a list. Reading item["price"] today is reading real API responses next week. And the parallel-lists bug - rice getting sugar's price - is a real production bug juniors get asked to fix. Bundles prevent it by construction.

project.title: Dukaan v0.5 - the stock book
project.brief: Amina's shop now has four items and she keeps mixing up the three parallel lists. Rebuild v0.5: the stock becomes one list of dictionaries. Every feature - the list, the bill, the alerts, the report - must work on the new shape. Deleting an item must be one operation, not three.

All v0.5 features work unchanged on the new shape.
New: remove an item by name in one operation; search prints one item's full record.
A note: one real mistake the old parallel lists could cause, in your own words.

milestones.check: Removal is one operation and cannot desynchronize.

title: Saving the shop
intro: Everything Dukaan knows lives in the program's memory. Close the program and it forgets - every morning Amina retypes the stock. Worse: one mistyped quantity crashes the whole bill. Today Dukaan v0.6 gets two upgrades: files give it a memory that survives closing, and try/except keeps it standing when input is bad.
objectives: Save a Python data structure to a file and load it back with the json module.
Use try/except to handle missing files and bad input without crashing.
Explain why JSON is the format programs use to share structured data.

concepts.title: Files remember after the program ends
concepts.text: Variables die when the program stops. A file survives. open("stock.json", "w") opens the file for writing; json.dump(stock, f) translates the list of dictionaries into text and writes it. Later, open("stock.json") with json.load(f) translates the text back into Python values. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation - a boring name for a useful idea) is text shaped exactly like Python lists and dicts, which is why the round trip is so smooth. "with" closes the file for you, even if something goes wrong inside the block.

concepts.title: Errors are messages, not the end
concepts.text: int("three") fails. A missing file fails. In Day 2 that meant a crash; today it means a decision. try: says "attempt this"; except ValueError: says "if that specific failure happens, do this instead." The program keeps running - it prints a helpful message, uses a safe default, and carries on. Catch specific errors (ValueError, FileNotFoundError), not everything: hiding all errors also hides your own bugs, and then nothing can be fixed.

concepts.title: JSON: the text format programs share
concepts.text: json.dump translates your list of dictionaries into text; json.load rebuilds it. The text is not Python - it is JSON, a format almost every language reads. That is why it matters beyond this lesson: on Day 9 you will read JSON from a real supplier API, and the file you save today is the same shape as the data that API sends. Keep the stock book to lists, dicts, text, and numbers - JSON cannot hold everything Python can.

example.run: Run python save.py from the starter directory. It creates and deletes its own demo file.
example.context: Amina's stock book, saved to a file and loaded back. The file might not exist yet - the program must not crash. Read the code, predict the exact output, then run it. Then, as an experiment: comment out the save block and run again - predict which branch runs.
example.code:
import json
import os

FILENAME = "dukaan_stock.json"

stock = [
    {"name": "Rice", "price": 250, "qty": 40},
    {"name": "Sugar", "price": 180, "qty": 90},
]

with open(FILENAME, "w") as f:
    json.dump(stock, f)
print("Saved the stock book.")

try:
    with open(FILENAME) as f:
        loaded = json.load(f)
    print(f"Loaded {len(loaded)} items: {loaded[0]['name']} and {loaded[1]['name']}")
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("No saved file yet - starting fresh.")
    loaded = []

typed = "three"
try:
    qty = int(typed)
except ValueError:
    print(f"'{typed}' is not a number - using 0.")
    qty = 0
print(f"Quantity accepted: {qty}")

os.remove(FILENAME)
print("Demo file cleaned up.")
example.output:
Saved the stock book.
Loaded 2 items: Rice and Sugar
'three' is not a number - using 0.
Quantity accepted: 0
Demo file cleaned up.
example.walkthrough: json.dump translates the stock list into text and writes it to dukaan_stock.json. The try block then reads it back: the file exists, so json.load rebuilds the list and the "Loaded 2 items" line prints - the except branch is skipped. Next, int("three") raises ValueError; the except catches it, prints the friendly message, and qty becomes 0 instead of crashing. Finally the demo deletes its own file so nothing is left behind. Now the experiment: comment out the save block and run again. This time open() raises FileNotFoundError, and you will see the "starting fresh" branch run. That branch is what v1.0 uses on every first launch.

exercises.title: Watch the missing-file branch
exercises.task: Comment out the save block (the "with open ... 'w'" part) and run. Predict what prints before you run.
exercises.hint: Without the save, the file does not exist when the load runs.
exercises.check: "No saved file yet - starting fresh." prints, and the program finishes normally.

exercises.title: Corrupt the file
exercises.task: In a scratch file, run only the load part after writing the text "hello" into dukaan_stock.json by hand. What error appears? Describe it in your own words.
exercises.hint: json.load on non-JSON text raises json.JSONDecodeError.
exercises.check: You can name the error and explain that the file's text was not valid JSON.

exercises.title: Round-trip your stock book
exercises.task: Build your 3-item stock book (a list of dicts), save it with json.dump, load it back, and print loaded == stock_book.
exercises.hint: == on two lists compares every value inside them.
exercises.check: It prints True - the round trip lost nothing.

mistakes: Catching every error with a bare "except:" - it hides your real bugs along with the expected failures.
Mixing up the file modes: json.dump needs the file opened for writing, json.load for reading.
Saving values JSON cannot hold and being surprised on load - keep the stock book to lists, dicts, text, and numbers.
fde: Two rules every junior learns the hard way. One: users type anything - "three", "-5", an empty line. A program that crashes on bad input is a bug report waiting to happen, and "handle invalid input gracefully" is one of the most common junior tickets there is. Two: data loss is the unforgivable bug. Losing Amina's stock book would be worse than any crash. Save carefully, load defensively, and never let a missing file become a lost morning.

project.title: Dukaan v0.6 - memory that survives
project.brief: Dukaan forgets everything when it closes - every morning Amina retypes the stock. Build v0.6: on start, load the stock book from dukaan_stock.json (or start fresh with a clear message if there is no file); after every change, save; and no bad input may ever crash it - "three", "-5", and empty input all get a friendly message.
deliverables: dukaan.py loads the stock book from dukaan_stock.json on start, or starts fresh with a message.
Adding an item saves the file immediately.
A test note: the bad inputs you tried and what the program printed.

milestones.title: Save the stock book
steps: After adding an item, json.dump the list to dukaan_stock.json.
Run twice and open the file - it holds your items.
Confirm the file is plain text you can read.
milestones.check: The file exists after the run and contains the items as JSON text.

milestones.title: Load it back
steps: On start, try to load the file; on FileNotFoundError start with a fresh list and a message.
Add an item, close, reopen - the item is still there.
Corrupt the file (write "hello" into it) and run - handle it without a traceback.
milestones.check: Stock survives a restart; a missing or corrupt file never crashes.

milestones.title: Unbreakable input
steps: Wrap every int(input(...)) in try/except ValueError.
Test with "three", "-5", and empty input.
Negative or zero quantities get a message, not a crash.
milestones.check: Every bad input prints a message; the program keeps running.

acceptance: Stock added in one run is present after closing and reopening.
First launch with no save file starts fresh with a clear message.
A corrupt save file produces a message and a fresh start, not a traceback.
Typing "three", "-5", or nothing at a quantity prompt shows a message, not a crash.
You can explain what try/except does in one sentence, using the missing file as the example.
tests: Friendly message, fresh start, no traceback
extensions: Keep a backup: before overwriting, copy the old file to dukaan_stock.bak.
Pretty-print the JSON with indent=2 so Amina can read the file herself.
review: Why is the load wrapped in try/except but the save usually is not?
What Python values can JSON not hold? What would break if the stock book used them?
Amina deletes the file by accident. What does she lose, and what would you change so she loses less?
